newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan opposition gains ground north of Kabul.
newsitem.headline: Afghan opposition gains ground north of Kabul.

text.p: Afghan opposition forces launched counter-attacks against the Taleban militia north of Kabul on Wednesday, gaining some ground in the key town of Jabal os-Siraj, a Pakistan-based news service said.
The Afghan Islamic Press (AIP) also quoted a Taleban spokesman saying that its opponents in nothern Afghanistan must release Taleban prisoners as a condition for talks peace talks offered by them.
It said forces loyal to former government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood had fought their way back into the northern part of the key town of Jabal os-Siraj, 70 km (45 miles) from Kabul.
But the Taleban, who captured Jabal os-Siraj on Tuesday, were still holding most of the town and the nearby Golbahar village at the mouth of Masood's Panjsher Valley stronghold.
Fighting subsided in the afternoon, with a new frontline running through the Dewari Bazaar area of Jabal os-Siraj.

In a separate development, an ammunition store exploded in Kabul on Wednesday, killing at least six Taleban fighters, according to AIP. Taleban authorities in the Afghan capital earlier denied there had been any casualties in the blast.
There was no immediate word on what had caused the explosion near the ancient Bala Hisar fort in southeastern Kabul.

Taleban spokesman Wakil Ahmad, quoted by AIP, said ethnic Uzbek authorities in the nothern city of Mazar-i-Sharif must release Taleban officials and hundreds of fighters taken prisoner when the militiia was ousted from there after heavy fighting last week.
The prisoners include Taleban Foreign Minister Mullah Mohamamd Ghous, northern commander Mullah Abdul Razzaq and central bank chief Mullah Ahsanullah.
Ahmad, speaking from the southern Afghan city of Kandahar, said release of prisoners would be a good omen for the future peace talks proposed by the opposition alliance.
AIP said Masood's men had launched a separate attack to try to regain positions they lost on Tuesday in the village of Pul-i-Matak, a few km (miles) south of Jabal os-Siraj.
Golbahar remained in Taleban hands, despite attacks by Masood's forces about five km (three miles) to the east.
AIP quoted Taleban sources as saying the purist Islamic militia was bringing reinforcements to the area.
Opposition spokesmen could not immediately be reached for comment and no first-hand account of the fighting was available.

The Taleban, who seized Kabul last September, launched a big offensive on Tuesday to recapture Golbahar and Jabal os-Siraj, which straddles the main highway linking Kabul to the north via the Salang Pass across the Hindu Kush mountains.

Masood had taken the two towns on Friday, cutting off a Taleban force that moved north of the Hindu Kush last week in an effort to link up with Taleban fighters who had established a fleeting presence in the northern capital of Mazar-i-Sharif.

They were expelled from Mazar-i-Sharif last Wednesday after heavy street fighting with a Shi'ite Moslem militia backed by ethnic Uzbek troops who had previously allied with the Taleban against opposition warlord General Abdul Rashid Dostum.
The mainly ethnic Pashtun Taleban, still the largest single force in Afghanistan, are determined to impose their strict Islamic rule throughout the war-shattered country.
In Islamabad, the Iranian embassy's cultural counsellor, Ali Zuelm, criticised the Taleban, without naming them, for trying to enforce their will on other groups in Afghanistan.

"Iran only recognises that administration in Afghanistan that has official international recognition," he told a news conference, referring to the government of president Burhanuddin Rabbani, ousted by the Taleban more than eight months ago.
On Monday, the Taleban shut down the Iranian embassy in Kabul and gave its staff 48 hours to leave, accusing them of spying and interference in Afghanistan's internal affairs.
Iran denied the charge and said the Taleban had closed the mission in reprisal for recent military setbacks at the hands of opposition forces, especially in northern Afghanistan.
